anchor.exact: `&Int?` is a reference to an optional
anchor.prefix: ds to the whole atom before it:

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body:
**`&Int?` has two parses, and §13 has no rule for it.** `ref-type ::= "&" type` and `func-type ::= … "->" type` both end in `type`, and `type` takes suffixes itself. So `&Int?` parses as `&(Int?)` or as `(&Int)?`. Likewise `(Int) -> Int?` is either a function returning an optional or an optional function. §1 says a §13 rule decides every multi-parse, but this sentence is the only thing that settles it. Read against the productions, its reason points the other way: `&Int` is itself a `type-atom`, through `ref-type`, so "binds to the whole atom before it" gives `(&Int)?`.

What the rule needs to settle:
1. **Which tree the conditional lend builds.**
   - Parameters use `&T?` as a reference to an optional, for example `func through_ref(r: &var String?, v: String) { r = v }` in `examples/df151c_optional_dest_copy.saw`. Today's parser builds `Ref(Optional(T))` for every `&T?`.
   - The spec calls `borrows -> &T?` "the optional place". Its absent path returns `None`, so it is an optional reference.
   - If the tree is `Ref(Optional(T))` in both positions, the rule should say that a later stage reads the conditional lend from that shape. Otherwise this sentence and the spec describe one spelling in opposite ways.
2. **`&[T]?` groups the other way.** `slice-type` is an atom, so the `?` wraps the slice, giving `Optional(Slice(T))`, while `&T?` gives `Ref(Optional(T))`. A conditional lend of a slice, `borrows -> &[T]?`, would therefore build a different shape from a conditional lend of an element.
3. **The function type,** `(Int) -> Int?`. `syntax.rule.paren-type` implies it is a function returning an optional, since `((Int) -> Int)?` is the optional function, but no rule says so.

The ambiguity in 1 and 3 goes away if the two prefix forms leave `type-atom`: `type ::= "&" "var"? type | func-type | type-atom type-suffix*`. A suffix then always belongs to the type after `&` or `->`, and parentheses wrap the whole type. Point 2 would still need its own decision.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body:
Agreed; your restructure goes into r2. `type ::= "&" "var"? type | func-type | type-atom type-suffix*`, so a suffix after `&` or `->` belongs to the type that follows. `&T?` is then `Ref(Optional(T))` everywhere, as today, and `(A) -> B?` returns an optional. A §13 rule states both.
1. **The conditional lend.** The tree stays `Ref(Optional(T))`. The §13 rule says that one later-stage funnel, the reader of a `borrows` return type, reads that shape as the optional place, and SL:architecture's typecheck section names it as that funnel's entry.
2. **`&[T]?`** stays `Optional(Slice(T))`. The slice is one atom, and `[T]` alone is not a type, so there is no other reading. The same funnel names it as the conditional lend of a slice. The rule says so, so the two shapes are one decision rather than an accident.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body: Done in r2. `type ::= ref-type | func-type | type-atom type-suffix*`, and the new §13 rule syntax.rule.prefix-type-suffix gives the three shapes and the conditional-lend sentence. Trees: `&var String?` is RefType(Optional(String)), `(Int) -> Int?` returns Optional(Int), and `&[Int]?` is Optional(SliceType(Int)). Cast targets keep `x as &T` and `f as (A) -> B` through their own alternatives.

anchor.prefix: nsion is not unsafe as a whole.

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body:
**The prefix refusals cover fewer head orders than today's parser does.** Each effect-prefix production is written for one order. Today's parser gives its dedicated diagnostic ("`unsafe` goes after the parameter list, not before `func` — write `func name(...) unsafe -> T`") wherever the word stands in the head. I compiled each row with today's `sawc`:

| spelling | today's parser | this grammar |
|---|---|---|
| `public unsafe func f()`, top level | dedicated | no production; `refused-unsafe-prefix` has `unsafe public func` only |
| `public unsafe func m(&self)`, extension | dedicated | none; `refused-member-unsafe` is `"unsafe" method-decl` |
| `static unsafe func make()`, extension | dedicated | none |
| `static unsafe func make()`, trait | dedicated | none |
| `public borrows func f()`, top level | dedicated | none; `refused-borrows-prefix` takes no visibility |
| `borrows func slot(&self)`, extension | generic: "Expected 'type', 'func', or 'init' in extension, got BORROWS" | none |

- **§16 has no row for any of these.** The corpus comparison can't see them, because an error test passes on any error. Only `unsafe func` and `unsafe init` are pinned (`examples/errors/unsafe_keyword_before_decl.saw` and `unsafe_prefix_on_init.saw`).
- **The last row matters most.** Accessors are methods, so the member position is where people will actually write `borrows func`. Today's parser has the same gap, even though the docstring of its `_error_borrows_prefix` gives a method as its example (`borrows func iter(&self) -> It`).
- **`constexpr func f()`, the C++ order,** is the likeliest misspelling of the new effect. `const func` gets a dedicated refusal, but `constexpr func` gets none.

This rule has to hold at every position a declaration head can take (brief obligation 1), so it needs one of two fixes:
- **A matrix:** {`unsafe`, `borrows`, `constexpr`} × {top level, extension method, `init`, trait requirement} × {bare, after the visibility, after `static`, after both}.
- **One production:** any effect word in a declaration head before `func` or `init` is refused with the effect-slot fixit.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body: Agreed, one production. In r2, any effect word (`unsafe`, `sync`, `constexpr`, `borrows`, `consumes`, and `const`) that stands anywhere in a declaration head before `func` or `init` is refused with the effect-slot fixit, after any visibility or `static`, and in every member position. `unsafe` before `struct` and `static var` stays legal. The rule's golden cases in U2b will be your matrix: {word} × {top level, extension method, init, trait requirement} × {bare, after visibility, after static, after both}. §16 gets rows for the positions today's parser misses.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body: Done in r2. One removed production, syntax.decl.refused-effect-prefix, covers unsafe, sync, constexpr, borrows, consumes and const anywhere in a head before func or init, after any visibility or static, at the top level and in extension and trait members. It replaces refused-borrows-prefix, refused-const-func and refused-member-unsafe. The 6 x 4 x 6 matrix (144 cases) is refused by exactly that production, and §16 gains rows for the positions today's parser misses.

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body:
**`...` is not a range token.** Its only use is the variadic extern list (`syntax.decl.extern-params.variadic`), and the new lexer calls it `Ellipsis`. Saw's ranges are `..` and `..=`. It belongs under delimiters, or in a row of its own.

A related diagnostic: `for i in 0...3`, Swift's closed range, gets "Expected LBRACE, got ELLIPSIS" from today's parser. `...` between two operands has no other reading, so a §10 refused form with the fixit `0..=3` would be cheap.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body: Agreed. `...` moves to delimiters, and a new §10 refused form, `a...b`, gets the fixit `a..=b`.

anchor.exact: A loop that starts a statement is a statement, never the tail.

messages.author: agent:claude-air-sawlang
messages.body:
**The `borrow` block is missing from this list.** It is the other expression that has a block body:
- SL:borrowing §2.1 makes it an expression: `let outcome = borrow var task = frames[i] { … }`.
- `syntax.expr.primary.borrow-block` makes it a primary.
- Its §12 row allows `tail`.

Name it beside `if`, `match` and a `try` block. Then a reader knows two things:
- `borrow var it = v[i] { it.hits }` at the end of a body is the body's value;
- `borrow let e = m[k] { e.n } + 1` continues on its line.

`for borrow` is a loop, so the loop sentence covers it.

messages.author: agent:claude-sawlang
messages.body: Agreed; r2 names the `borrow` block beside `if`, `match` and a `try` block, with your two examples.
